title: Biomechanical Characterization of Human Soft Tissues Using Indentation and Tensile Testing
protocol: Manually dissect off the adipose tissue and the thin layer of deep dermis from skin specimens using a scalpel blade and forceps.
Cut the resulting sheet of split-thickness skin into standardized sample sizes (e.g., 1 cm × 5 cm).
Dispose of used scalpel blades in appropriate sharps bins.
Orientate skin samples in the same direction (e.g., perpendicular or in-line with Langer Lines).
Immobilize the sample between two clamps on a commercial jig.
Affix one clamp to a 98.07 N load cell and the other to an immovable base plate.
Ensure the tested area between the clamps is 1 cm x 4 cm.
Cover the sample area with petroleum jelly on both sides after placement in the apparatus.
Program the tensile loading and relaxation testing regime into the software as follows: Zero Load | Zero Position | Find Contact (Tensile loading) | Wait (Relaxation).
Start the test using the programmed software.
Load the sample under tension to 29.42 N at a rate of 1 mm/s.
After reaching 29.42 N, allow the tissue to relax for 1.5 hours.
Maintain constant displacement during the relaxation phase.
Calculate elastic and viscoelastic properties as per the analysis section guidelines.
Remove skin and fascia from the cartilage specimen using a scalpel blade and forceps.
Divide the cartilage specimens into standardized 1.5-cm blocks using a scalpel blade and forceps.
Use a semicircular-shaped indenter with a diameter at least 8 times greater than the size of the cartilage sample for indentation testing.
Dispose of used scalpel blades in appropriate sharps bins.
Measure the thickness of the cartilage before mechanical testing using electronic calipers.
Cover the cartilage sample with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) prior to and during compression testing to ensure hydration.
Compress the hydrated cartilage samples using a materials testing machine at room temperature.
Orientate the cartilage sample so the surface is perpendicular to the indenter.
Program the compressive loading and relaxation testing regime into the software as follows: Zero Load | Zero Position | Find Contact (Compressive loading) | Wait (Relaxation).
Start the test using the software program.
Load the sample under compression to 2.94 N at 1 mm/s.
Allow the cartilage to relax for 15 min after reaching the 2.94-N limit.
Collect raw data including time (s), displacement (mm), and load (N) from the materials testing device.
Calculate the stress (MPa) and strain (%) using provided formulas.
Plot a linear scatter plot of stress MPa against strain %.
Determine the linear curve fit for the plotted data.
Ensure all data points are included to achieve an R value >0.98.
Identify the slope, which corresponds to Young's Modulus indicating compressive resistance or tension resistance in MPa.
Calculate the ratio of stress over time during the last 200 seconds of testing.
Determine the final stress level at the end of the experiment to identify viscoelastic properties.
Assess the fast stress-relaxation response if fluid flow has reached equilibrium.
Plot stress in MPa against time in seconds on a linear scatter plot.
Determine a linear curve fit to calculate the rate of relaxation.
Calculate the m value from the equation y = mx + b using data points from the last 200 seconds.
Ensure all data points are included to achieve an R value >0.98.
Record the final stress (MPa) at 1.5 hours for skin samples as the absolute relaxation value.
Record the final stress (MPa) at 15 minutes for cartilage samples as the absolute relaxation value.
